claims.text: Ludovico Bertonio’s Aymara–Spanish dictionary bears a Juli, Chucuito, 1612 imprint. Behind the named Jesuit author stood Indigenous Aymara writers: his introduction describes their compositions about Christian teachings, saints and sermons. Bertonio extracted words and expressions from those writings to build the dictionary.
claims.explanation: The title page names Juli, but the physical location of printing has been debated. The vocabulary’s regional emphasis does not make it a complete record of every Aymara variety.

claims.text: The book was intended to help priests teach, preach and hear confessions in Aymara. Bertonio praised the collaborators’ command of the language and urged learners to consult skilled speakers, practice writing and study Aymara texts. The vocabulary especially reflects Lupaca usage in Chucuito. Its pages therefore preserve Indigenous literary and linguistic work within a colonial mission project, as well as the church’s practical dependence on local language expertise.

claims.text: Between about 1700 and 1715, Dominican priest Francisco Ximénez copied the Popol Vuh in Chichicastenango, Guatemala. The surviving manuscript places K’iche’ written in Latin letters alongside his Spanish translation. It preserves K’iche’ Maya accounts of creation, origins, traditions and spiritual history, making the text itself a record of how a sacred narrative was transmitted across languages.
claims.explanation: The exact relationship between this copy, earlier written versions and oral recitation remains under study. The Newberry guide gives 1700–1715; the linked catalog suggests a narrower probable date for its larger manuscript volume.

claims.text: The handwritten pages contain corrections to the K’iche’ text, and their form reflects a tradition intended for oral presentation. The Newberry Library’s guide describes a possible earlier, sixteenth-century version written by an Indigenous author using Latin letters. The surviving copy later traveled from Guatemala to Europe and then Chicago, where it entered the Newberry collection in 1912. Its eighteenth-century date belongs to this manuscript, while the stories and traditions it carries are older.
